reasoning_summary: Based on recent U.S. adult marital and cohabitation patterns, about half of adults are married, a smaller share live with an unmarried partner, around one in ten are in a non-cohabiting relationship, and roughly one-third are not currently in a relationship.

Based on Census/Pew benchmarks: roughly half of U.S. adults are married (~48-50%), about 8-9% cohabit with an unmarried partner, roughly 8-10% report a non-cohabiting romantic relationship, and about a third report no current relationship (including widowed, divorced, and never-married singles).

Estimates extrapolated from recent Census/ACS marital status and Pew ATP partnership data (married ~48-51%, cohabiting ~7-9%); remainder split using typical committed-noncohabiting vs. unpartnered adult shares, held roughly stable to 2026.

Estimated from recent U.S. household composition patterns: roughly 30-32% of adults live in a household with children under 18. Among those households, older children only are most common, with smaller but similar shares having only young children or both young and older children.

About one-third of U.S. adults live in a household with children under 18 (household-with-children share ~30-40%, and adults with kids are concentrated in ages 25-49). Among those, most have school-age-only children; younger-child-only households are fewer, and mixed-age households fewer still.

Estimating from recent Census/CPS/ACS figures adjusted to adults (not households) and slight 2026 aging/fertility decline: ~70% of U.S. adults live in HH with no minors. Of the ~30% who do, steady-state age spacing and parity distributions imply roughly 9% only <6, 14% only 6-17, and 7% both.

Estimated from recent U.S. household income distributions, adjusted for nominal income growth by 2026 and for an adult-weighted survey sample, which shifts somewhat more adults into higher-income households than a household-weighted distribution.

Based on Census household income distribution (median ~$80k in 2024-25), roughly a third of households are under $50k, ~28-29% between $50k-$100k, ~18% $100k-$150k, and ~20% at $150k+. Survey respondents (adults, weighted) skew marginally higher-income than households overall, and item nonresponse is excluded here.

Based on recent Census ACS/CPS household income distributions (median ~$80k in 2023), inflation-adjusted forward to 2026, and typical right-skew: ~30% under $50k, ~28% in $50-100k, ~18% in $100-150k, ~24% at $150k+.

National attitudes suggest marriage is meaningful for many U.S. adults but no longer viewed as essential to a fulfilling life by a majority. A sizable share would rate it somewhat important, while the rest split between low and no importance.

Pew-style items on what matters for a fulfilling life consistently show marriage rated lower than job/career, close friends, or children; only roughly a quarter to a third call it very important, with a large minority saying it is not too/not at all important (driven by unmarried, younger, and previously married adults). A 4-point scale without a neutral option pushes some mass to 'somewhat'.

Based on long-term U.S. trends of delayed/declining marriage, rising singlehood, and generational shifts (younger adults de-emphasizing marriage), roughly 40% view it as unimportant while ~60% still rate it somewhat/very important; slight tilt toward 'very' among older cohorts yields this 2026 adult distribution.

Raising children is likely seen as highly meaningful by many parents and some prospective parents, but a sizable minority of U.S. adults are childless or do not view parenthood as central to fulfillment.

Pew-style items on what matters for a fulfilling life show children rank well below job/career and friendships, with only about a quarter to a third rating it at the top on a 5-point scale. Collapsing to a 4-point scale shifts more mass into 'Very important,' but a substantial minority (childfree adults, older adults past that stage, younger adults deprioritizing parenthood) place low importance. Expect a bimodal-ish spread with a plurality at 'Very important'.

Based on recent Pew/Gallup trends in US family values, declining fertility ideals, and personal fulfillment surveys (where parenthood ranks high but not universally essential amid rising childfree rates), estimated ~42% view raising kids as very important to their own fulfillment, with the rest tapering off.

Most U.S. adults are likely to see paid-work or career success as at least somewhat tied to a fulfilling life, but the share saying it is very important is moderated by retirees, nonworkers, caregivers, and adults who prioritize family, health, or personal autonomy over career achievement.

Most U.S. adults value work/career success, but the wording emphasizes 'success' (more competitive framing) and the sample includes retirees, homemakers, and those prioritizing family, so the top box is high but not dominant; 'Somewhat' absorbs a large share. Prior Pew-style items show ~70-80% rating career fulfillment at least somewhat/very important.

U.S. adults typically rate career/paid-work success as a core (if secondary to family) component of a fulfilling life in value surveys; thus low shares dismiss it while a plurality call it very important and most of the rest somewhat important.

Most U.S. adults are likely to reject the idea that childcare should fall mainly to one parent, favoring either an equal split or a flexible arrangement based on circumstances. The broad 'depends on the family' option would attract many respondents because it accommodates work schedules, preferences, and practical constraints.

Americans strongly endorse egalitarian ideals for childcare, so 'divide about equally' should dominate (~45-50%). 'Depends on the family' is a common hedge (~20-25%), 'parent with more available time' is a pragmatic option drawing ~20-25%, and only a small traditionalist minority (~6-8%) says one parent should do most of it.

Egalitarian norms dominate U.S. opinion on parenting; equal sharing is the modal preference, followed by pragmatic time-availability, with smaller shares for traditional one-parent primacy or pure relativism.

Most U.S. adults are likely to endorse an egalitarian division of routine housework, though many would qualify this by available time or household-specific circumstances; few would say one person should generally do most of it.

Americans strongly endorse egalitarian norms in housework; 'divide about equally' should dominate, followed by the time-availability rationale and 'depends on the household' as a hedge. Very few endorse one person doing most of it.

US adults increasingly favor egalitarian norms for housework per long-running Pew/GSS trends on gender roles; equal-sharing is modal, followed by pragmatic time-availability, residual situational flexibility, and low support for one-sided traditional loads.

Most U.S. adults are likely to favor an egalitarian norm for major household financial decisions, with a smaller share saying it depends on the specific decision. Few would endorse authority based mainly on earning more or handling day-to-day money management.

U.S. adults overwhelmingly endorse egalitarian joint decision-making for major household finances; norm-consistent 'both together' dominates, with 'it depends' a modest second, and very few endorsing higher-earner or money-manager authority.

Egalitarian norms dominate modern U.S. views on household finances; joint decisions are strongly preferred for major choices, followed by situational flexibility. Hierarchical options (higher earner or money manager) attract only small minorities.

U.S. adults would likely favor a family-specific approach over a single rule, with substantial support for sharing reductions equally or using job flexibility; fewer would choose the lower earner rule because it can seem economically practical but less egalitarian.

Explicit 'it depends' options draw heavy support on normative family-tradeoff questions, likely a plurality (~35-40%). Among substantive rules, 'more flexible job' reads as practical and gender-neutral, while 'both reduce equally' appeals to egalitarian respondents (especially younger/liberal); 'lower earner' is economically intuitive but sounds like it disadvantages women, so it lags.
Egalitarian norms favor equal sharing as fairest; pragmatism boosts flexibility and 'depends' options; pure economic logic (lower earner) least endorsed amid dual-earner realities.
